n1-licao-condominio.enunciado:
A Kubernetes cluster is a condo: several buildings (the nodes, the machines) and a management office (the control plane). The apartments are the pods: where the containers live.

The management office (and who works there)

To help you remember, each component became a character whose name starts like the component’s:

CharacterComponentWhat they do
Apolinário, the doormanAPI ServerEvery request goes through him: yours (via kubectl) and the other components’. He checks it and writes it down.
Etelvina, the archivistetcdKeeps the book with everything in it: what exists, how it should be, who lives where.
Shirley, the real-estate agentSchedulerPicks which building each new apartment goes in, based on available space.
Conceição, the inspectorController managerCompares desired with actual, all the time, and orders the difference fixed.
Kleber, the caretakerkubeletOne in each building: creates and watches the containers in his building’s apartments.

The path of a request

  1. You call Apolinário on the intercom (kubectl): “I want a pod with nginx”.
  2. He checks the request and writes it in Etelvina’s book.
  3. Shirley sees an apartment with no building and picks one with room.
  4. That building’s Kleber sees the new apartment, downloads the image and starts the container.

In the simulator, the management office lives on the control-plane node. See it with kubectl get pods -n kube-system: there you’ll find etcd, the API Server, the scheduler and the controller manager.
n1-licao-condominio.vidaReal: The cluster is a condo: several buildings (nodes) and a management office (the control plane) that takes care of everything.
n1-licao-condominio.limite: In a real condo, each resident picks the building. Here the management office picks, and the apartment (pod) never changes buildings: if the building goes down, a new apartment is born somewhere else.

n1-licao-pod-yaml.enunciado:
Everything in Kubernetes is described in a manifest (YAML) with four parts:

  • apiVersion: the API version (Pod is v1; Deployment is apps/v1);
  • kind: the object type;
  • metadata: the name, the namespace and the labels;
  • spec: how you want it to be.

Once applied, the object gets one more part, the status, which the cluster itself writes: it’s the “how it is right now”. Compare kubectl get pod ola -o yaml with the file in the editor.

In YAML, indentation (2 spaces, never TAB) says what’s inside what, and - starts a list item (each container is an item of containers).

To finish: click ▶ Apply and then ⬆ Submit. Also try kubectl get pods and kubectl describe pod ola.
n1-licao-pod-yaml.vidaReal: The manifest is the apartment’s blueprint: it says how it should be, not how to build it.
n1-licao-pod-yaml.limite: A wrong blueprint can be rejected by the doorman (a field that doesn’t exist) or accepted and cause trouble later (an image that doesn’t exist).

n1-licao-kubectl.titulo: kubectl: the intercom to the doorman
n1-licao-kubectl.enunciado:
The commands you’ll use every day:

CommandWhat for
kubectl get podsLists them (add -o wide to see IP and node, -A for all namespaces).
kubectl describe pod NAMEThe full record, with the Events at the end: the incident log.
kubectl logs NAMEThe container’s diary (what the program wrote).
kubectl exec NAME -- COMMANDRuns a command inside the container (stepping into the apartment).
kubectl apply -f FILECreates or updates from the blueprint (YAML).
kubectl delete pod NAMEDeletes it.
kubectl explain pod.specThe manual for every field.

Reading kubectl get pods

NAME   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
web    1/1     Running   0          2m
  • READY: ready containers / total in the pod.
  • STATUS: Running, Pending (no spot yet), ContainerCreating, CrashLoopBackOff (crashing and coming back), ImagePullBackOff (the image didn’t download)...
  • RESTARTS: how many times the container has restarted. A rising number is a sign of trouble.
  • AGE: how long the pod has existed.

In this site’s terminal, the Tab key completes commands and names, and ↑ repeats the previous command.
n1-licao-kubectl.vidaReal: kubectl is the intercom: you talk to the doorman (API Server), never directly to the buildings.
n1-licao-kubectl.limite: The intercom only works if you know the resident’s right name (and the company’s: the namespace).

n1-quantos-nodes.titulo: How many buildings does the condo have?
n1-quantos-nodes.enunciado: Use the terminal to find out how many nodes the cluster has, counting the control plane. Write the number in the field below.
n1-quantos-nodes.vidaReal: Counting the condo’s buildings, including the management office’s.
n1-quantos-nodes.limite: Condo buildings don’t vanish; nodes join and leave the cluster (and, in the cloud, they can be created on demand).

n1-primeiro-pod.titulo: Laying the cornerstone: the first pod
n1-primeiro-pod.enunciado:
Complete the file to create a Pod:

  • named recepcao;
  • with a container named web, from the nginx:1.27 image.
n1-primeiro-pod.dica: kind: Pod · metadata.name · spec.containers: - name / image
n1-primeiro-pod.vidaReal: The condo’s first apartment: an address with a resident inside.
n1-primeiro-pod.limite: A standalone apartment, with no contract (Deployment), isn’t rebuilt if it disappears. In the next level you’ll see how to fix that.

n1-kubectl-run.titulo: A pod straight over the intercom
n1-kubectl-run.enunciado: Without writing YAML, create a pod from the terminal named porteiro with the httpd:2.4 image.
n1-kubectl-run.vidaReal: Ordering an apartment by phone, without drawing the blueprint: quick for testing.
n1-kubectl-run.limite: An order by phone isn’t saved in a file: to repeat it tomorrow, or in another cluster, the blueprint (YAML) is better.

n1-em-que-node.titulo: Which building does the mystery live in?
n1-em-que-node.enunciado: The misterio pod is running on some node. Find out which one and write the node’s name.
n1-em-que-node.dica: -o wide adds the IP and NODE columns. describe shows it too.
n1-em-que-node.vidaReal: Finding out which building in the condo an apartment is in.
n1-em-que-node.limite: Here the “building” was picked by the real-estate agent (the scheduler), not by the resident. To pin a specific building there are dedicated rules (level 7).

msgs.0: you looked at the node in kubectl (-o wide, describe or jsonpath)

n1-diario.enunciado: The diario pod writes everything to its log. One of the entries has the construction site’s Wi-Fi password. What is it?
n1-diario.vidaReal: The construction log: everything that happened is written down there.
n1-diario.limite: The container’s log disappears when the pod is deleted. To really keep it, logs get shipped somewhere else.

n1-cofre.titulo: Get into the apartment and open the safe
n1-cofre.enunciado:
Inside the container of the cofre pod, in the /cofre folder, there’s a file with the combination. Find out what it is.

You can run a single command (kubectl exec cofre -- ls /cofre) or open a shell (kubectl exec -it cofre -- sh, and exit to leave).
n1-cofre.vidaReal: Stepping into the apartment to look in a drawer.
n1-cofre.limite: Poking around inside the container is good for investigating, but whatever you change there disappears when the pod is recreated.

msgs.0: you got into the container (kubectl exec)

n1-labels.enunciado:
The balcao pod needs two labels:

  • app: loja
  • time: vendas

After applying, try a search by label: kubectl get pods -l time=vendas.
n1-labels.dica: metadata.labels is a map: key: value, one per line.
n1-labels.vidaReal: Signs on the door say whose apartment it is: “team: sales”.
n1-labels.limite: Labels aren’t unique: several apartments can have the same one, and whoever searches by that label gets all of them.

testes.descricao: the label search finds the pod

n1-seletor.titulo: How many are on the support team?
n1-seletor.enunciado: Some pods have the equipe (team) label. How many pods have equipe=suporte? Use kubectl’s label selector.
n1-seletor.dica: kubectl get pods -l key=value (and --show-labels shows all the labels)
n1-seletor.vidaReal: “Every apartment with the label equipe: suporte.”
n1-seletor.limite: The selector doesn’t know the actual “team”, only the label. A pod with the wrong label is left out (or sneaks in uninvited).

n1-namespaces.titulo: Two companies, the same meeting room
n1-namespaces.enunciado:
Create two namespaces, financeiro (finance) and rh (HR), and a pod named sala-de-reuniao (image nginx:1.27) in each one.

In a single file, separate the objects with ---. Then take a look: kubectl get pods -A.
n1-namespaces.dica: kind: Namespace only needs metadata.name. In the pod, metadata.namespace says where it lives.
n1-namespaces.vidaReal: Each company in the condo can have its own “sala-de-reuniao”: the name repeats, but the full address, with the company, doesn’t.
n1-namespaces.limite: A namespace separates names, but on its own it locks nothing: one company’s pods still talk to the other’s.

n1-contexto.titulo: Work directly in the sales company
n1-contexto.enunciado: Typing -n vendas in every command gets tiring. Change your kubectl’s default namespace to vendas (sales). After that, a plain kubectl get pods should show the caixa pod.
n1-contexto.vidaReal: Setting up the intercom to ring the sales company directly, without saying its name every time.
n1-contexto.limite: It’s just a shortcut in your kubectl: other users keep their own namespace.
n1-contexto.comoSaber: kubectl config get-contexts shows vendas in the NAMESPACE column.

n1-dry-run.enunciado:
Writing YAML from scratch is slow. kubectl generates the draft for you, without creating anything:

  1. generate the YAML of a rascunho (draft) pod with the nginx:1.27 image using --dry-run=client -o yaml and save it to the rascunho.yaml file (with > rascunho.yaml);
  2. apply the file.

The file shows up in the editor: you can tweak it before applying. (On the CKAD exam, this trick saves a lot of time.)
n1-dry-run.vidaReal: Asking the management office for a pre-filled draft blueprint, instead of drawing one from scratch.
n1-dry-run.limite: The draft only comes with the basics: you still complete the blueprint before ordering the build.

n1-explain.enunciado: You want the container’s program to run in a specific folder. Use kubectl explain to find which container field sets the working folder.
n1-explain.vidaReal: The management office’s technical manual: every blueprint field explained.
n1-explain.limite: The manual says what each field is, not which value to use in your case.

n1-colegas.enunciado:
Create the dupla (pair) pod (label app: dupla) with two containers:

  • web: nginx:1.27;
  • assistente: busybox:1.36, with the command sleep 3600 (without a command that keeps running, busybox exits right away).

READY should show 2/2. To see the logs of one of them or step into it, use -c NAME.
n1-colegas.dica: command: ["sleep", "3600"] in the second item of containers.
n1-colegas.vidaReal: Two residents sharing the same apartment: the main tenant and an assistant.
n1-colegas.limite: Pod roommates are born, move and die together: you can’t scale just the assistant.

n1-intruso.titulo: There’s an intruder in the building
n1-intruso.enunciado: A pod named intruso showed up in the default namespace. Delete it (and only it).
n1-intruso.limite: Deleting a pod is final: it doesn’t come back, because nobody (no contract) asked for it to exist.

testes.descricao: the intruder left and the others stayed

n1-vitrine.enunciado: The vitrine (shop window) pod is stuck. Investigate with kubectl describe (look at the Events at the end) and fix it: it should run nginx, version 1.27.
n1-vitrine.dica: In a pod, the image can be swapped: kubectl set image pod/vitrine vitrine=...
n1-vitrine.vidaReal: The vitrine’s prefab module never arrived: someone wrote the wrong model on the order.
n1-vitrine.limite: Here you fix the order yourself; in a Deployment, the right way is to fix the YAML and apply it again.
